candidate.answerReason: Reflecting each die face r to 7-r pairs sums 1994 and 7n-1994. The value 337 is attained when n=333. An injective comparison into a proper subset proves that every feasible sum below 337 has strictly smaller probability than 1994.

methods.label: Reflect the faces and exclude smaller sums
methods.explanation:
Replacing every die face \(r\) by \(7-r\) gives a useful symmetry. This replacement is its own inverse, and it changes a sum \(u\) into \(7n-u\). Thus sums \(u\) and \(7n-u\) have the same probability.

Since \(332\cdot6=1992<1994\), positive probability for a sum of \(1994\) requires \(n\ge333\). When \(n=333\), the reflected sum is
\[
7\cdot333-1994=337.
\]
A sum of \(337\) is possible with \(332\) ones and one five. Its reflected roll has sum \(1994\), so \(337\) is an attainable value of \(S\).

To prove that it is smallest, suppose an integer \(S<337\) had the same positive probability as \(1994\). Every die contributes at least \(1\), so
\[
333\le n\le S\le336.
\]
Set \(T=7n-1994\). By reflection, \(T\) has the same probability as \(1994\), and the four possible values of \(n\) give
\[
337\le T\le358.
\]
We will show that there are strictly more rolls with sum \(T\) than with sum \(S\).

Label the dice so that a roll is an ordered list. In any roll with sum \(S\), each face is at most
\[
S-(n-1)\le336-332=4.
\]
There is therefore room to increase any chosen face by \(1\). Let \(k=T-S\). We have \(1\le k\le25<n\). Add \(1\) to each of the first \(k\) dice. The resulting roll is valid and has sum \(T\). Different original rolls give different resulting rolls, because subtracting \(1\) from those same dice recovers the original roll.

Every resulting roll has its first die at least \(2\). However, there is also a roll of sum \(T\) whose first die is \(1\): let
\[
d=T-n=6n-1994.
\]
Here \(4\le d\le22<n\), so we may set \(d\) of the other dice to \(2\) and all remaining dice to \(1\). Its sum is \(n+d=T\), and it is outside the constructed image.

Thus strictly more ordered rolls have sum \(T\) than sum \(S\). All ordered rolls for the same \(n\) are equally likely, so \(P(T)>P(S)\), contradicting their required equality. Therefore the smallest possible value is \(\boxed{337}\), choice C.

candidate.annotationRationale: The task-level target is an attained discrete minimum, requiring both a construction and exclusion of all smaller values. Face reflection gives a bijection between equal-probability events. The strict comparison is a bijection onto a proper subset, with an explicit omitted roll. Equally likely outcomes and integer bounds support the method; no recurrence is used.

review.mathematicalCheck: Face reflection pairs sums u and 7n-u and attains S=337 at n=333. For S<337, positivity forces 333≤n≤S≤336. The stated increment map injects sum-S rolls into sum-T rolls, and the constructed first-die-1 roll lies outside its image, proving strictly greater probability for T and excluding every smaller S.
